prompt: **Problem 1.2.1.** We work in ZFC (axioms of extensionality, pairing, union, power set, separation, infinity, replacement, regularity, choice); *regularity* says every nonempty set $X$ has an element $x$ with $y\notin x$ for all $y\in X$. Given a nonempty set $X$, prove that there exists a set $\bigcap X$ such that $y\in\bigcap X$ iff $y\in x$ for all $x\in X$.
answer: Use separation inside one element of $X$.

solutions.title: Separation
solutions.body: Pick $x_0\in X$ ($X\ne\varnothing$). By the axiom of separation there is a set $T=\{y\in x_0:\ \forall x\in X\ (y\in x)\}$. If $y\in T$ then $y\in x$ for all $x\in X$. Conversely, if $y\in x$ for every $x\in X$, then in particular $y\in x_0$ and $y$ satisfies the condition, so $y\in T$. Thus $T$ is the required set. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.2.3.** In set theory the *ordered pair* is defined by $(x,y)=\{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}$. Prove that $(x,y)=(z,w)$ if and only if $x=z$ and $y=w$.
answer: Compare elements using extensionality; treat $x=y$ separately.

solutions.title: Case analysis
solutions.body:
($\Leftarrow$) is immediate. ($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $\{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}=\{\{z\},\{z,w\}\}$.

*$x=z$.* $\{x\}$ lies in the right side, so $\{x\}=\{z\}$ or $\{x\}=\{z,w\}$. In both cases $z\in\{x\}$, so $z=x$.

*$y=w$.* Now $z=x$. If $x\ne y$: the set $\{x,y\}$ has two elements, so it is not equal to $\{z\}=\{x\}$; hence $\{x,y\}=\{x,w\}$, and $y\in\{x,w\}$ with $y\neq x$ forces $y=w$. If $x=y$: the left side is $\{\{x\}\}$, so $\{z,w\}=\{x\}$ and $w=x=y$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 1.2.6.** We work in ZFC (axioms of extensionality, pairing, union, power set, separation, infinity, replacement, regularity, choice); *regularity* says every nonempty set $X$ has an element $x$ with $y\notin x$ for all $y\in X$. Prove that no set contains itself, and that no two sets contain each other (there are no $x,y$ with $x\in y$ and $y\in x$).

solutions.title: Use regularity
solutions.body:
*No set contains itself.* The set $\{x\}$ (pairing) is nonempty, so it has an $\in$-minimal element, which can only be $x$; minimality says no element of $\{x\}$ belongs to $x$, i.e. $x\notin x$.

*No 2-cycles.* Suppose $x\in y$ and $y\in x$. The set $\{x,y\}$ has an $\in$-minimal element. If it is $x$, then no element of $\{x,y\}$ lies in $x$, but $y\in x$: contradiction. If it is $y$, then $x\notin y$: contradiction. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.1.** A set $x$ is *transitive* if $z\in y\in x$ implies $z\in x$. A set $\alpha$ is an *ordinal* if $\alpha$ is transitive and every element of $\alpha$ is transitive. For ordinals, $\alpha<\beta$ means $\alpha\in\beta$ and $\alpha\le\beta$ means $\alpha\subseteq\beta$; the successor is $S(\alpha)=\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$. Show that every element of an ordinal is an ordinal.
answer: Elements of $\alpha$ are transitive, and their elements lie in $\alpha$, hence are transitive.

solutions.title: Unfold the definition
solutions.body: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal and $\beta\in\alpha$. By definition of ordinal, $\beta$ is transitive. If $\gamma\in\beta$, then $\gamma\in\alpha$ because $\alpha$ is transitive, so $\gamma$ is an element of $\alpha$ and therefore transitive. So $\beta$ is a transitive set all of whose elements are transitive: an ordinal. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.7.** A set $x$ is *transitive* if $z\in y\in x$ implies $z\in x$. A set $\alpha$ is an *ordinal* if $\alpha$ is transitive and every element of $\alpha$ is transitive. For ordinals, $\alpha<\beta$ means $\alpha\in\beta$ and $\alpha\le\beta$ means $\alpha\subseteq\beta$; the successor is $S(\alpha)=\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$. You may use that if $\alpha,\beta$ are ordinals then $\alpha\subseteq\beta$ iff $\alpha\in\beta$ or $\alpha=\beta$, and that elements of ordinals are ordinals. Prove that $S(\alpha)=\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$ is the least ordinal greater than $\alpha$.
answer: $S(\alpha)$ is an ordinal containing $\alpha$, and any ordinal $\beta\ni\alpha$ contains $S(\alpha)$ as a subset.

solutions.title: Check and compare
solutions.body:
*$S(\alpha)$ is an ordinal.* Transitive: if $x\in S(\alpha)$ then $x\in\alpha$ (so $x\subseteq\alpha\subseteq S(\alpha)$) or $x=\alpha\subseteq S(\alpha)$. Its elements are transitive: elements of $\alpha$ are ordinals, and $\alpha$ itself is transitive.

*Greater than $\alpha$:* $\alpha\in S(\alpha)$.

*Least:* if $\beta$ is an ordinal with $\alpha<\beta$, i.e. $\alpha\in\beta$, then $\alpha\subseteq\beta$ (transitivity of $\beta$) and $\{\alpha\}\subseteq\beta$, so $S(\alpha)\subseteq\beta$, i.e. $S(\alpha)\le\beta$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.2.1.** A set $x$ is *transitive* if $z\in y\in x$ implies $z\in x$. A set $\alpha$ is an *ordinal* if $\alpha$ is transitive and every element of $\alpha$ is transitive. For ordinals, $\alpha<\beta$ means $\alpha\in\beta$ and $\alpha\le\beta$ means $\alpha\subseteq\beta$; the successor is $S(\alpha)=\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$. A *limit ordinal* is a nonzero ordinal which is not a successor $S(\beta)$. The supremum of a set of ordinals is its union. Show that a nonzero ordinal $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal iff $\alpha=\sup\{\beta:\beta<\alpha\}$ ($=\bigcup\alpha$). You may use: for ordinals, $S(x)\le\alpha$ whenever $x<\alpha$; $\gamma\subseteq\alpha$ iff $\gamma\in\alpha$ or $\gamma=\alpha$; and no set contains itself and no two sets contain each other.
answer: Compute $\bigcup S(\beta)=\beta$; for limit $\alpha$ show $x<\alpha\Rightarrow S(x)<\alpha$.

solutions.title: Both directions
solutions.body:
$\bigcup\alpha\subseteq\alpha$ always, as $\alpha$ is transitive.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $\alpha$ be a limit ordinal and $x\in\alpha$. Then $S(x)\le\alpha$, i.e. $S(x)\in\alpha$ or $S(x)=\alpha$. The latter would make $\alpha$ a successor, so $S(x)\in\alpha$. As $x\in S(x)\in\alpha$, we get $x\in\bigcup\alpha$. Hence $\alpha\subseteq\bigcup\alpha$ and $\alpha=\bigcup\alpha$.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\alpha\neq0$, $\alpha=\bigcup\alpha$ and, for contradiction, $\alpha=S(\beta)=\beta\cup\{\beta\}$. Then $\beta\in\alpha=\bigcup\alpha$, so $\beta\in\gamma$ for some $\gamma\in\alpha$. Either $\gamma=\beta$, giving $\beta\in\beta$, or $\gamma\in\beta$, giving $\beta\in\gamma\in\beta$ (two sets containing each other). Both are impossible. So $\alpha$ is not a successor: it is a limit ordinal. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.2.4 (transfinite induction).** A set $x$ is *transitive* if $z\in y\in x$ implies $z\in x$. A set $\alpha$ is an *ordinal* if $\alpha$ is transitive and every element of $\alpha$ is transitive. For ordinals, $\alpha<\beta$ means $\alpha\in\beta$ and $\alpha\le\beta$ means $\alpha\subseteq\beta$; the successor is $S(\alpha)=\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$. Let $C$ be a class. Suppose that for every ordinal $\alpha$: if $\beta\in C$ for all $\beta<\alpha$, then $\alpha\in C$. Prove that $C$ contains all ordinals. (You may use that every nonempty class of ordinals has a least element.)
answer: Take the least ordinal not in $C$.

solutions.title: Least counterexample
solutions.body: Suppose some ordinal is not in $C$. Then $D=\{\alpha\in\mathrm{Ord}:\alpha\notin C\}$ is a nonempty class of ordinals, so it has a least element $\alpha_0$. Every $\beta<\alpha_0$ is an ordinal not in $D$ (by leastness), hence $\beta\in C$. By the hypothesis, $\alpha_0\in C$, contradicting $\alpha_0\in D$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.3.1.** A *well-ordered set* $(X,<)$ has an irreflexive transitive relation $<$ with any two distinct elements comparable and every nonempty subset having a minimal element. An *order-isomorphism* $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection with $x<_Xy\Rightarrow f(x)<_Yf(y)$; write $X\cong Y$. Show: (a) $X\cong X$; (b) $X\cong Y\Rightarrow Y\cong X$; (c) $X\cong Y$ and $Y\cong Z$ imply $X\cong Z$.

solutions.title: Check each property
solutions.body:
(a) The identity map is an order-isomorphism.

(b) Let $f:X\to Y$ be an order-isomorphism; $f^{-1}$ is a bijection. Let $u<_Yv$ and suppose $f^{-1}(u)\not<_Xf^{-1}(v)$. By comparability, $f^{-1}(u)=f^{-1}(v)$ (then $u=v$, contradicting irreflexivity of $<_Y$) or $f^{-1}(v)<_Xf^{-1}(u)$, whence $v<_Yu$; with $u<_Yv$ transitivity gives $u<_Yu$, a contradiction. So $f^{-1}$ preserves order.

(c) If $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ are order-isomorphisms, $g\circ f$ is a bijection and $x<y\Rightarrow f(x)<f(y)\Rightarrow g(f(x))<g(f(y))$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.2.** For a set $X$, $|X|$ is the least ordinal $\alpha$ with $X\approx\alpha$ (a bijection exists); an ordinal $\kappa$ is a *cardinal* if $|\kappa|=\kappa$, and *infinite* if $\kappa\ge\omega$. Prove that every infinite cardinal is a limit ordinal.

solutions.title: Shift an element away
solutions.body:
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. If $\kappa=\omega$ it is a limit ordinal. Otherwise $\kappa>\omega$; suppose $\kappa=S(\beta)=\beta\cup\{\beta\}$. Since $\omega<\kappa$, we get $\omega\le\beta$.

Define $f:\beta\cup\{\beta\}\to\beta$ by $f(\beta)=0$, $f(n)=n+1$ for natural numbers $n$, and $f(\gamma)=\gamma$ for $\omega\le\gamma<\beta$. It is a bijection. So $\kappa\approx\beta$ with $\beta<\kappa$, contradicting $|\kappa|=\kappa$. Thus $\kappa$ is not a successor, and being nonzero it is a limit ordinal. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.5.** Using the definitions $|X|=$ least ordinal equinumerous to $X$, and *cardinal* $=$ ordinal $\kappa$ with $|\kappa|=\kappa$: prove that if $X$ is a set of cardinals then $\sup X=\bigcup X$ is a cardinal. Conclude that $\omega$ is a cardinal (you may use that every natural number is a cardinal and $\omega=\sup$ of the natural numbers). You may use the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem.
answer: If $|\lambda|=\mu<\lambda$, some $\kappa\in X$ has $\mu<\kappa\le\lambda$; then $\kappa\approx\mu$ by Schröder–Bernstein.

solutions.title: Squeeze with Schröder–Bernstein
solutions.body:
Let $\lambda=\bigcup X$ and suppose $\mu=|\lambda|<\lambda$. Then $\mu\in\lambda$, so $\mu\in\kappa$ for some $\kappa\in X$, i.e. $\mu<\kappa\le\lambda$.

We have $\kappa\subseteq\lambda\approx\mu$, so there is an injection $\kappa\to\mu$; and $\mu\subseteq\kappa$ gives an injection $\mu\to\kappa$. By Schröder–Bernstein $\kappa\approx\mu$ with $\mu<\kappa$, contradicting that $\kappa$ is a cardinal. So $\lambda$ is a cardinal.

Since $\omega=\sup\{n:n<\omega\}$ and each $n$ is a cardinal, $\omega$ is a cardinal. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.1.6.** The aleph numbers are defined by $\aleph_0=\omega$; $\aleph_{\alpha+1}=$ the least cardinal greater than $\aleph_\alpha$; $\aleph_\alpha=\sup\{\aleph_\beta:\beta<\alpha\}$ for limit $\alpha$. (All $\aleph_\alpha$ are cardinals and $\alpha<\beta\Rightarrow\aleph_\alpha<\aleph_\beta$.) Prove that every infinite cardinal equals $\aleph_\alpha$ for some ordinal $\alpha$.
answer: Take the least $\alpha$ with $\aleph_\alpha\ge\kappa$ and do cases: $0$, successor, limit.

solutions.title: Least $\alpha$ with $\aleph_\alpha\ge\kappa$
solutions.body:
First, $\aleph_\alpha\ge\alpha$ for all $\alpha$ (transfinite induction: $\aleph_0=\omega\ge0$; $\aleph_{\beta+1}>\aleph_\beta\ge\beta$ gives $\aleph_{\beta+1}\ge\beta+1$; at a limit $\alpha$, $\aleph_\alpha=\sup_{\beta<\alpha}\aleph_\beta\ge\sup_{\beta<\alpha}\beta=\alpha$). Hence $\aleph_\kappa\ge\kappa$, and there is a least $\alpha$ with $\aleph_\alpha\ge\kappa$.

- $\alpha=0$: $\omega\ge\kappa\ge\omega$ (as $\kappa$ is infinite), so $\kappa=\omega=\aleph_0$.
- $\alpha=\beta+1$: $\aleph_\beta<\kappa$ by minimality of $\alpha$, so $\kappa$ is a cardinal greater than $\aleph_\beta$, hence $\kappa\ge\aleph_{\beta+1}$ (the least such). With $\aleph_{\beta+1}\ge\kappa$ we get $\kappa=\aleph_{\beta+1}$.
- $\alpha$ limit: $\aleph_\beta<\kappa$ for all $\beta<\alpha$, so $\aleph_\alpha=\sup_{\beta<\alpha}\aleph_\beta\le\kappa\le\aleph_\alpha$. So $\kappa=\aleph_\alpha$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.2.5.** You may use Hessenberg's theorem $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$ for infinite cardinals $\kappa$, and monotonicity of cardinal sum and product. Show that if $\kappa,\lambda$ are nonzero cardinals and at least one is infinite, then $\kappa+\lambda=\kappa\cdot\lambda=\max\{\kappa,\lambda\}$.

solutions.title: Sandwich
solutions.body:
By symmetry assume $\kappa\le\lambda$, so $\lambda$ is infinite and $\max=\lambda$. Since $\kappa\ge1$:
$$\lambda\le\kappa+\lambda\le\lambda+\lambda=2\cdot\lambda\le\lambda\cdot\lambda=\lambda,\qquad\lambda=1\cdot\lambda\le\kappa\cdot\lambda\le\lambda\cdot\lambda=\lambda.$$
Hence $\kappa+\lambda=\kappa\cdot\lambda=\lambda$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 3.2.7.** For cardinals $\kappa,\lambda$, $\kappa^\lambda=|\mathrm{Hom}(\lambda,\kappa)|$ (the set of functions $\lambda\to\kappa$), and $|\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)|=|Y|^{|X|}$. Show that $|\mathcal P(X)|=2^{|X|}$ for every set $X$.

solutions.title: Characteristic functions
solutions.body: Map $A\subseteq X$ to its characteristic function $\chi_A:X\to\{0,1\}=2$, $\chi_A(x)=1$ iff $x\in A$. This is a bijection $\mathcal P(X)\to\mathrm{Hom}(X,2)$ with inverse $f\mapsto f^{-1}(\{1\})$. Hence $|\mathcal P(X)|=|\mathrm{Hom}(X,2)|=2^{|X|}$. $\blacksquare$
